newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - US funds "star system" still going strong.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - US funds "star system" still going strong.

text.p: When Magellan Fund manager Jeff Vinik resigned from Fidelity Investments last year, many proclaimed that the 'star system' of promoting managers was over.
Fidelity executives have downplayed the loss of Vinik and other well-known mutual fund managers by stressing the strengths of its enormous research staff.
Yet flip through any newspaper or business magazine and the faces of mutual fund managers stare back, and more of them seem to be switching companies.
"The star system ain't gone," said Morningstar Mutual Funds publisher John Rekenthaler. "Purely and simply, it's a managers' market in terms of their value to employers right now."

Warburg Pincus Funds snatched Brian Posner, manager of Fidelity's $14.8 billion Equity-Income II Fund, in early December in the hope that his strong track record would bring additional funds and prestige to the company.
Newspaper advertisements show a picture of Posner with his name in big letters and the remind to readers: "It's easy to transfer your IRA to Warburg Pincus Funds."

Analysts said investors pulled about $200 million from Posner's Fidelity fund in December. His new fund, Warburg's Growth & Income, has shown relatively no increase in assets since he took over about three weeks ago, but analysts suggested it just may take time.

Almost like free agents in sports, fund managers are commanding seven-digit salaries, a piece of the company and more control in corporate affairs, said Larry Lieberman, president of mutual fund headhunters Wadsworth Associates, who recruited Posner.

"It's like baseball rotisserie time," Lieberman said. "People are investing with (fund managers) as much as the companies they are investing in. Very few managers are not taking our calls at the moment."

Robertson Stephens Investment Management recruited Jim Callinan from Putnam Funds last year and has promoted him aggressively in ads as the star manager of their Emerging Growth Fund. WHAT THE ATTRACTIONS ARE
Robertson Stephens spokesman Jeff Hawkins said the fund company lures and retains money managers by offering them a piece of the company.
"A lot of them do become partners in the firm," he said. "A lot of the managers could go off and run hedge funds, like Vinik. Others could go off and start their own fund companies."
Many fund managers who leave large fund companies such as Fidelity like the freedom and adaptability of managing a smaller fund, where small cap stocks can have a bigger impact, Rekenthaler said.

Vinik is widely-regarded as a master at picking small companies with strong growth trends, but when managing the $50 billion Magellan Fund, he was forced to buy large cap stocks like Chrysler Corp, General Motors Corp and Intel Corp.
Since forming his own hedge fund, he has gone back to buying small cap stocks, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
"He was running a bloated, huge, enormous fund. There's every expectation that he'll whack the daylights out of the ball at a smaller fund," said George Van, chairman of Van Hedge Fund Advisors.
More than a dozen fund managers have left Fidelity since the beginning of last year, which at the very least makes retail and institutional investors nervous, analysts said.
"People don't like change when it comes to their money," said Don Dion, publisher of Fidelity Independent Advisor, which tracks Fidelity funds.
WILL CHANGES HURT PERFORMANCE? Analysts are divided over
whether the numerous changes in fund managers at Fidelity in the last year will hurt performance.

Some point out that, up until recently, Magellan continued to outperform the market after star manager Peter Lynch resigned in 1990. Other Fidelity funds have also bettered their peer group despite changes in managers.
However David O'Leary, president of Alpha Equity Research, worries that some managers are being promoted beyond their experience levels.

Bettina Doulton, who has been managing funds for almost four years, heads two funds, Fidelity Equity-Income II Fund and Fidelity Puritan Fund, whose combined assets of more than $33 billion would make it among the largest of mutual funds.
"That's my fear, that they're losing all their experienced people," said O'Leary. "They don't have a lot of grey temples."
O'Leary and Dion agree that Fidelity and other fund companies who want to hold onto their top managers will have to reassess compensation issues.
In August 1995, Fidelity chairman Ned Johnson surrendered his family's voting control of the huge fund company to its top 50 executives and a few fund managers to help ensure loyalty.

"I think most of the portfolio managers who left over the past year are not shareholders of Fidelity, although I believe Vinik was," Dion said. "We're not happy with all of this turnover, and we think Fidelity has to start paying better salaries."
